Equilateral On Lines

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: three straight lines each hold one point, and we try to slide the points until they make an equilateral triangle.
How to play: Drag C, C1 or C2 along its line, or drag a line up and down; you can also focus a point and use the arrow keys or press the line buttons. Tick Show hint to see the two answers.
Look for the math

Three parallel lines, one point on each: can the three points always be made into an equilateral triangle? The old applet answers with a turn of 60 degrees, and draws the two possible answers when you ask for a hint.

A turn of 60 degrees

Hold C fixed. If ABC is equilateral, turning point A about C through 60° lands exactly on B: the turn is a rotation, so it keeps the distance to C and changes the direction by 60°. Turn line L1 about C through the same angle and call the new line L′. A goes with its line, so the image of A lies on L′. It is also B, which lies on L2. Therefore B is where L′ meets L2, and A is found by turning B back.

Why the triangle must be equilateral

With A on line L1 at height y1, C on L0 at y0 and B on L2 at y2, write d1 = y1 - y0 and d2 = y2 - y0. Turning by s · 60° with s = +1 or -1 gives

y2 - y0 = s · sin(60°) · (Ax - Cx) + cos(60°) · d1

Because sin(60°) is not zero, this equation has one solution for Ax for each sign: with C fixed there are exactly two answers, one turned clockwise and one counterclockwise. The construction gives CA = CB and ∠ACB = 60°, so the third side is equal too. In the special case where L1 is midway between L0 and L2, the two triangles share B; when L2 is midway, they share A. They are still different, differently oriented triangles.

What the checks found

The logic test tries 210 sets of three line heights with five places for C, and both directions: 2,100 constructed triangles. Every one has A on L1, B on L2, three equal sides (worst difference 1.1 × 10-13 pixels) and a 60° angle at C (worst error 4.4 × 10-16 radians). It also writes the applet's own Compute() a second time from its bytecode and agrees in all 4,696 layouts, including the 3-pixel snap and the order in which the two answers are tried. So the page's claim is confirmed. One stray phrase in the article, "Then ΔABC is equilateral, scalene, right, equilateral, obtuse", is a leftover from a different question; the stated puzzle and the proof both give an equilateral triangle, and this port follows those. The live article now embeds GeoGebra; the Java applet is preserved in a 2014 Wayback snapshot, which describes the draggable points C, C1 and C2.

Where C can go

C itself slides along its line, so each new position gives a fresh pair of answers: there are infinitely many triangles across the whole picture, but only two for a fixed C. If two of the lines are moved together the triangle can collapse, and the old applet's intersection test even reports a missing point when two lines are parallel after a rotation. The article says the idea also works when the lines are not parallel; that wider case is not tested here.

Try Shuffle lines, then tick Show hint: the two triangles sit on opposite sides of C, and the Rotation slider shows what happens before the turn reaches 60°.
